sections.html:
• Other names: Dwarf Swordtail, Slender Pygmy Swordtail
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (about 40 litres)
  • Breeding: easy to medium
  • Dwellers: top and middle
  • Nitrate: less than 80
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Lifespan: up to 5 years
  • Colour forms: yellow, blue

The Pygmy Swordtail is a very small freshwater fish belonging to the family Poeciliidae. The typical adult size ranges from 1 to 1.5 inches (2.5 to 3.8 cm) in length.

Size. On average, males are approximately 2.5 to 3 cm long. In rare cases, males can reach almost 3.8 cm, but these are exceptions, as experiments have shown that they do not pass on the corresponding gene responsible for size to their offspring. Females are slightly larger than males, on average 29–40 mm.

Besides this species, Xiphophorus continens and Xiphophorus multilineatus are also classified as smaller swordtails.

Coloration. The main coloration is greyish-brown. The belly is lighter in color. This species has no vertical bars. In females, there is often one bold lateral line running from the eye along the body.

Color genotypes. There are two genotypes of males in this species:

  • yellow
  • blue

In reality, they are called “blue” only as a convention, because their color is not actually blue, but rather has brown nuances (this is their wild color). Among the yellowish ones there can also be brightly colored individuals, which is why some researchers consider them a third type, but this has not yet been recorded in scientific literature.

Females are duller blue-gray with a yellow tint on the dorsal side.

Swords. Xiphophorus pygmaeus has a highly reduced sword or none at all. It may sound strange, but in this species most males do not exhibit a prominent sword-like structure; only a smaller proportion of males possess one. At the base of the caudal fin there can be a very short sword, generally less than 2 mm but never more than 8 mm. The sword does not have black edging.

Fins. The dorsal fin is relatively small, both in height and in length at the base. The fin is transparent, with a subtle black border and a faint black stripe that runs one-third of the way up the fin.

Lifespan. There is currently no data on the maximum lifespan of Xiphophorus pygmaeus in the wild. In aquariums, Pygmy Swordtails typically live 3–5 years if appropriately cared for. It is important to provide them with a suitable environment, a balanced diet, and regular maintenance to ensure their well-being and longevity.

Xiphophorus pygmaeus is a freshwater species endemic to Mexico and occurs exclusively in the Rio Axtla and its tributaries (Rio Tancuilin and Rio Huichihuayan) within the Pánuco River system.

According to studies, this species is abundant in Rio Huichihuayan, and less common in the lower 9 km of Rio Tancuilin and the upper 5 km of Rio Axtla.

These fish inhabit clear, shallow waters (less than 1 m deep), within well-shaded, moderately to fast-flowing spring-fed streams. They prefer areas with undercut banks and dense stands of submerged aquatic vegetation.

Despite their small size, a group of 6–8 fish requires an absolute minimum aquarium size of 10 gallons (40 litres). There are several important reasons for this:

  • These fish are pretty active and move around a lot.
  • If you have several males, there will be aggression because of limited space.
  • It is hard to create current in small tanks.
  • Maintaining water balance and parameters is easier in larger aquariums because they provide a larger volume of water.
  • This allows for more stable water conditions and dilutes any potential fluctuations in water chemistry.

Pygmy Swordtails are jumpers, so it is imperative to take measures such as using a tank cover, lowering the water level, and using floating plants to ensure their safety.

To ensure the well-being of Pygmy Swordtails, it is essential to understand their needs and create an environment that closely resembles their natural habitat.

Pygmy Swordtails are pretty delicate fish. They are particularly sensitive to ammonia, nitrites and nitrates.

Therefore, it is highly recommended to avoid introducing them as the first inhabitants immediately after the aquarium cycling process is completed. It is recommended to wait at least a few weeks to allow a stable and balanced environment to establish.

Temperature: 22–26°C (71–78°F).

pH: These fish prefer slightly alkaline conditions. The ideal pH range is 7.0–8.0.

Hardness: The recommended general hardness (GH) range is 8 to 20 dGH. They do not like soft water.

Water flow: In their natural habitat, Pygmy Swordtails inhabit shallow waters with moderate or relatively fast current, and they like to swim in it. Although it is possible to keep these fish in an aquarium without a current, it is still advised to create a current if you want to offer ideal conditions.

Lighting: Pygmy Swordtails thrive in subdued lighting. If you keep these fish in planted tanks, however, lighting should be adapted to the needs of the plants.

Aeration: Aeration and water flow often go hand in hand. A powerful filtration system needs to be in place to aerate the water properly and maintain a high level of oxygenation, as the fish enjoy well-oxygenated water. Air stones and other aeration decorations can be added to the tank for more oxygen.

Decorations and plants: Pygmy Swordtails are shy and appreciate plenty of hiding places, such as caves, driftwood, tall plants and floating plants. They may retreat to these places if they feel threatened or stressed. It is not recommended to keep these fish in open aquariums, as an open layout is unsettling for these timid fish.

Dwarf water lettuce, frogbit, duckweed and other floating plants are excellent at diffusing light and providing the subdued lighting these fish prefer.

This species is a diurnal omnivore. Pygmy Swordtails are not picky eaters; they will happily eat dry and freeze-dried foods such as flakes, pellets and crisps, as long as the food suits their mouth size.

In the aquarium, they can be fed a wide variety of foods such as:

  • spirulina,
  • brine shrimp (Artemia salina),
  • Artemia nauplii,
  • daphnia,
  • fruit flies,
  • moina,
  • detritus worms,
  • vinegar eels,
  • mosquito larvae,
  • cyclops, etc.

How to feed: This is a diurnal species, so it is better to feed them in the morning. Use the “five-minute rule”. Ideally, feed in small portions (at least 2 times a day) rather than a large amount once a day. This mimics their natural feeding behavior and helps prevent overfeeding and digestive issues.

Diet type: omnivore. Food preference: meat. Feeding frequency: daily.

Plant safe: Yes, Pygmy Swordtails are completely plant safe. They will not eat healthy plants in the tank and do not eat living plant material.

Temper: Pygmy Swordtails are peaceful fish. Although males establish dominance hierarchies and compete for access to females, their agonistic interactions with each other almost never escalate into physical contact. It is generally recommended to keep only one male with several females, or to keep a group of males with plenty of space and hiding places to reduce such behavior. Unlike their larger cousins, even when stressed they usually do not nip the fins of long-finned or slow-moving fish. They are pretty shy and are easily scared off.

Activity: They are relatively active and lively if no fish bully them. They enjoy exploring their environment and are particularly fond of areas with dense vegetation or places to hide. They are also good jumpers, so you need to cover the tank or lower the water level by at least a few centimetres (about 5–8 cm).

Sociality: Swordtails are social fish. It is recommended to keep them in groups of at least 3–4 individuals to ensure their well-being and encourage natural behavior; ideally at least 3–4 females per male. Being in a group reduces stress and improves their overall well-being. Do not introduce just a pair (one male and one female) into a tank: the female would be constantly harassed and pursued by the male, which exhausts, stresses and weakens her.

Placement in the tank: They tend to occupy the upper and middle sections of the tank, with occasional visits to the bottom, though they do not particularly favor the bottom area.

  • Social: yes
  • Activity: moderate
  • Placement: top and middle dwellers
  • Peaceful: yes
  • Nippers: no
  • Jumpers: yes

Tankmates: Pygmy Swordtails are friendly fish suited to smaller tanks, but make sure they still have sufficient swimming space. When choosing tankmates, consider size, behavior and compatibility; for example, it is best to avoid keeping them with territorial fish that like to assert control over the aquarium.

Fish: In community tanks, tankmates should be small species that are not big enough to eat or harass them. Ideally choose species that prefer warm, slightly alkaline water, such as neons, Endlers, zebra danios (Danio rerio), guppies, pygmy corydoras, least killifish (Heterandria formosa), swordtails, ghost glass catfish, butterfly hillstream loaches, Borneo suckers, medaka ricefish, etc.

Shrimp: It is possible to keep Pygmy Swordtails with dwarf shrimp. These fish have mouths too small to threaten adult or even juvenile shrimp. However, newly hatched shrimp are tiny enough (2 mm) to fit in their mouths, so there is always a chance they will snack on them from time to time. Shrimplets a few weeks old are too big for them to eat.

Snails: They are compatible with any freshwater snail.

Avoid:

  • Large and/or aggressive and/or boisterous fish.
  • All types of crayfish and most types of freshwater crabs.
  • Even small African dwarf frogs can and will try to catch them whenever possible.

Males are slightly smaller than females (about 2.5–3 cm versus 2.9–4 cm) and have a gonopodium, a modified anal fin. Some males have a very short sword at the base of the caudal fin. Females often show one bold lateral line from the eye along the body and are duller blue-gray with a yellow tint on the dorsal side.

Breeding Pygmy Swordtails is a relatively easy process, similar to other livebearers. For breeding, keep a ratio of 1 male to 3–4 females.

Maturity: This species reaches maturity at around 5–6 months of age.

  • Males are considered mature when the gonopodium is fully formed (third, fourth and fifth anal fin rays elongated and fused) and the pectoral fins are fully pointed.
  • Females can be identified by a brood spot.

Mating:

  • In this species there is no courtship. Even abnormally large males exhibit only chasing behavior. A male performs a parallel approach, swimming closely parallel to the female.
  • According to one study, with lower predation risk, females showed mating preferences for blue males, but yellow males dominated in agonistic interactions and were more aggressive in pursuing females. However, females from the population with high predation risk showed no preference for blue males.
  • There is no sexual selection by females.
  • Females also prefer the large courting males of Xiphophorus nigrensis to their own small, non-courting males. Given a chance, females prefer larger conspecifics to small conspecifics.
  • Xiphophorus pygmaeus can easily hybridize and produce viable offspring with other Xiphophorus species (such as X. cortezi and X. nigrensis).

Fertilization: Fertilization is internal. Males use a sexual organ called a gonopodium to introduce sperm into the female’s oviduct.

Gestation: Depending on the temperature, the gestation period is 3–4 weeks.

Fecundity: Xiphophorus pygmaeus is not a prolific breeder, contrary to what some sources say. This is probably because of their small size and relatively large fry. On average, females give birth to only 3–4 fry.

Fry: Newborn fry are fairly large (6–7 mm). They require microscopic food such as infusoria, moina, artemia, or specialized liquid or powdered products. In the wild, Xiphophorus pygmaeus almost never see their offspring, as the fry are immediately swept away by the current. In aquariums, the parents may mistake the fry for food, but this species does not deliberately hunt down and chase its fry, so in most cases the fry survive. Nonetheless, to ensure their survival the aquarium should be densely planted, or the fry should be kept in a separate tank for at least a month.

The genus name “Xiphophorus” is derived from two Greek words: “xiphos”, meaning “sword”, and “phoros”, meaning “bearer” or “carrier”. The species name “pygmaeus” is of Greek origin, meaning “dwarf” or “tiny”, and shows the miniature size of this fish.

In 1943, Xiphophorus pygmaeus received its name from Hubbs and Gordon because, during its description, they observed all known males of this species to be smaller than males of closely related swordtail species.

Pygmy Swordtails are not as popular as common swordtails, so many people miss out on the unique beauty and personality of this tiny species. This small, colorful fish can be a highlight in many peaceful community aquariums, especially planted tanks.
